title: Two Teenagers Opened Fire at a San Diego Mosque, Killing Three. For South Asian Muslims in America, It Hits Close to Home
excerpt: The attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego — the county's largest mosque — is being investigated as a hate crime. For the Indian and Pakistani diaspora in the US, it is a reminder that places of worship remain targets.
body:
On Monday afternoon, two teenagers dressed in camouflage walked into the Islamic Center of San Diego and opened fire. Three men were killed. The shooters — aged 17 and 18 — then drove a few blocks away and killed themselves.

San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl said the department is investigating the attack as a hate crime. There was no specific threat made against the mosque, but investigators found evidence that the suspects had engaged in what Wahl called "generalized hate rhetoric." He declined to elaborate, saying more details would emerge in the coming days.

Among the dead was Amin Abdullah, a security guard who had worked at the mosque for more than a decade. Police said his actions were "heroic" and likely prevented a much worse outcome. "Undoubtedly he saved lives today," Wahl said. Abdullah's family friend, Shaykh Uthman Ibn Farooq, said the guard had chosen the role specifically because "he wanted to defend the innocent."

The attack unfolded even as police were already searching for one of the teenagers. His mother had called authorities earlier that morning, reporting her son was suicidal and had run away. Weapons were missing from the home, and her car was gone. Officers used automated license plate readers and other technology to track the vehicle, but reports of the shooting came in before they could intervene.

Police responded within four minutes. As they arrived at the mosque, gunshots rang out a few blocks away, where a landscaper was shot at but uninjured. The two suspects were found dead in a vehicle stopped in the middle of a road.

## A Community Under Siege

The Islamic Center of San Diego is the largest mosque in San Diego County. It houses the Al Rashid School, which offers Arabic language and Islamic studies for children as young as five. Aerial footage showed more than a dozen children being walked out of the parking lot, holding hands, surrounded by scores of police vehicles.

Imam Taha Hassane, the mosque's director, called the attack "extremely outrageous." He noted that the center focuses on interfaith relations and community building — a group of non-Muslims had been touring the mosque to learn about Islam just hours before the shooting.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) condemned the attack. "No one should ever fear for their safety while attending prayers or studying at an elementary school," said CAIR-San Diego Executive Director Tazheen Nizam.

President Donald Trump called the shooting a "terrible situation."

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the roughly 3.5 million Muslims of South Asian origin living in the United States — Indians, Pakistanis, Bangladeshis, and Sri Lankans — attacks on mosques carry a particular weight. Many attend mosques that serve as the social and cultural heart of their communities, where children learn Urdu or Arabic alongside religious studies, where Eid celebrations bring together families from across metropolitan areas.

The San Diego attack comes against a backdrop of rising hate crimes targeting Muslim Americans. FBI data has consistently shown mosques and Islamic centres among the most frequently targeted religious institutions in the country. For NRIs and PIOs who chose the United States partly for its promise of religious freedom, each such incident forces a reckoning with the gap between that ideal and the reality on the ground.

Security at mosques has become a growing concern — and a growing expense — for communities that often operate on modest budgets. Many have had to install cameras, hire guards, and conduct active-shooter drills. The heroism of Amin Abdullah underscores both the danger these communities face and the quiet courage of those who stand between worshippers and harm.

## What Comes Next

Police said the investigation is ongoing. The identities of the suspects have not been publicly released, given that one was a minor. Authorities are examining the suspects' digital footprints and communications to understand the full extent of their radicalization.

For the Islamic Center of San Diego, Monday's violence will leave scars that outlast the news cycle. The mosque has said it will continue its interfaith programs and community work — but the children who were led out of that parking lot, hand in hand, will carry this memory for a long time.
